findings.headline: The Financial Implications section gives the proposals' value as up to £986k, while Table 1 and paragraph 2.16 give £976k.
findings.detail: The Financial Implications split of £586k firm and £390k uncertain adds to £976k, which matches Table 1. The £986k figure in the Financial Implications section therefore does not match the table total.
findings.matters: A finance officer reconciling the committee paper against the budget model would need to know which total the council is relying on before approving the package.
findings.figures: £986k (Financial Implications section); £976k (Table 1 total); £586k (firm); £390k (further)
findings.quote: The proposals would reduce the 2027/28 revenue budget gap by up to £986k, of which £586k is firm and £390k carries greater uncertainty.

findings.headline: The £141k budget process figure is net of £230k of potential savings from fleet fuel, commercial income and IT, and an £89k finance system cost pressure.
findings.detail: The paper describes the £230k as potential savings. The £89k is a cost pressure for the finance system. Both sit within the wider budget process, which the paper says is ongoing and will be refined.
findings.matters: The net figure depends on savings that are described as potential, and a finance director can test the gross and net numbers against their own budget-process savings.
findings.figures: £141k (net budget process figure); £230k (potential savings); £89k (finance system cost pressure)
findings.quote: The budget process figure is the net of potential savings of £230k (fleet fuel, commercial income and IT) and a cost pressure of £89k for the finance system.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs are not yet reflected in the 2027/28 figures and are assumed to stay at current levels.
findings.detail: The paper lists temporary accommodation costs among items not yet reflected in the figures. The risk register rates rising temporary accommodation demand as medium likelihood and high impact, with demand monitoring and early reporting as mitigations.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation demand is a cost that can rise quickly and sits outside the current gap, which other councils with housing pressures will want to compare against.
findings.figures: None given
findings.quote: temporary accommodation costs, which are assumed to stay at current levels.

findings.headline: LGR costs are not included in the 2027/28 figures, with Local Government Reorganisation now paused.
findings.detail: The paper says the funding review assumed district councils would have been reorganised into unitary authorities by its third year, and that this assumption no longer holds because LGR is paused. It says district councils across the sector face budget pressures as a result.
findings.matters: Unquantified reorganisation costs sit outside the gap, and the funding assumption behind the settlement has changed, which affects how peer councils and lenders read the MTFS.
findings.figures: None given
findings.quote: LGR costs are not included in the current figures and remain a risk.

findings.headline: Removing out-of-date projects from the capital programme would reduce borrowing by £0.9m and save an estimated £90k a year in MRP and interest.
findings.detail: The proposal is to approve removal of the projects listed in Appendix 4, which is not included in this document. The paper says the saving will be confirmed against asset lives and borrowing rates in that appendix, and that the proposal reduces the Capital Financing Requirement.
findings.matters: Cutting planned borrowing lowers the Capital Financing Requirement and the MRP and interest charged to revenue, which is a borrowing decision a lender and a peer finance officer would both track.
findings.figures: £0.9m (reduction in borrowing); £90k a year (estimated MRP and interest saving)
findings.quote: reducing borrowing by £0.9m and saving an estimated £90k a year in MRP and interest.

findings.headline: Without the proposals, the Budget Stabilisation Reserve would fall to £332k by the end of 2027/28, be exhausted during 2028/29, and leave a shortfall of £1,455k.
findings.detail: With the proposals, the paper says the reserve funds the 2027/28 and 2028/29 gaps and leaves £497k for 2029/30. The paper states that using reserves buys time but is not a sustainable way to balance the budget.
findings.matters: The reserve path with and without the package shows how quickly a council's general reserve cover runs down when the gap is not closed, which is the core question for finance directors and lenders.
findings.figures: £332k (reserve at end 2027/28 without proposals); £1,455k (shortfall without proposals); £497k (reserve left for 2029/30 with proposals)
findings.quote: The reserve would fall to £332k by the end of 2027/28 and would be exhausted during 2028/29, leaving a shortfall of £1,455k.

findings.headline: A £300k planning income stretch target is proposed, which the paper says depends on larger, less frequent applications.
findings.detail: The target is classed as a further proposal and the paper says it carries more risk than the other proposals. The risk register rates the target as not achieved with medium likelihood and high impact. Any shortfall would fall on the Budget Stabilisation Reserve in the first instance.
findings.matters: A stretch income target that is largely unevidenced at this stage is a common route to later budget overspends, and a shortfall would draw directly on reserves.
findings.figures: £300k (planning income stretch target, 2027/28); £300k (further proposal value)
findings.quote: This depends on larger, less frequent applications and on the wider economy, so it carries more risk than the other proposals.

findings.headline: Counting the firm proposals alone, the 2027/28 gap would be £1,024k before budget process savings.
findings.detail: The firm proposals total £586k: car parking and Northam Burrows charges (£300k), the statutory planning fee increase (£200k) and the garden waste subscription increase (£86k). The further proposals total £390k: the planning income stretch target (£300k) and capital programme rationalisation (£90k).
findings.matters: The split shows how much of the package rests on decisions and income that are not yet certain, which matters to any reader judging the reliability of a council's savings plan.
findings.figures: £586k (firm proposals); £390k (further proposals); £1,024k (2027/28 gap on firm proposals, before budget process savings); £300k; £200k; £86k; £90k
findings.quote: On a prudent basis, counting only the firm proposals, the 2027/28 gap would remain at £1,024k before the budget process savings.

findings.headline: The five proposals and £141k of budget process savings would reduce the 2027/28 gap from £1,610k to £493k.
findings.detail: The proposals total £976k in 2027/28. The paper says the same measures reduce the 2028/29 gap from £1,928k to £811k. The remaining gaps are planned to be met from the Budget Stabilisation Reserve.
findings.matters: This is the package the council is asking Full Council to approve to close the gap, and it sets the residual reserve draw that other councils can compare against their own plans.
findings.figures: £976k (proposals, 2027/28); £141k (net budget process savings); £1,610k to £493k (2027/28 gap); £1,928k to £811k (2028/29 gap)
findings.quote: Taken together with £141k from the wider budget process, the proposals reduce the 2027/28 gap from £1,610k to £493k

findings.headline: The 2027/28 budget gap is £1,610k, against £1,362k in the February 2026 MTFS.
findings.detail: The gap has grown since February 2026 for further pressures: £90k of additional borrowing costs for the town hall, a £30k staff pay award, and £128k from raising the 2027/28 pay award assumption from 2% to 3%. The paper says the gap is more than 10% of a net revenue budget of approximately £13m.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare the rise in the gap with their own MTFS assumptions, and a lender can see the scale of unfunded pressure against the revenue base.
findings.figures: £1,610k (2027/28 gap); £1,362k (February 2026 MTFS gap for 2027/28); £90k (town hall borrowing costs); £30k (staff pay award); £128k (3% pay award assumption); £1.6m; approximately £13m (net revenue budget)
findings.quote: The updated budget gap for 2027/28 is £1,610k.

findings.headline: Investments in 'green treasury deposits' are given priority where the reduction in yield against standard deposits is within 0.2%.
findings.detail: Green deposits must meet the council's investing limits and credit requirements and the cash flow timescales. The paper sets a maximum yield reduction of 0.2% at an annual rate for them to qualify.
findings.matters: A yield tolerance for ethical deposits sets a clear trade-off between return and policy aims that other councils may be considering.
findings.figures: 0.2% (maximum reduced yield at an annual rate)
findings.quote: Any reduced yield when comparing to standard treasury deposits is within 0.2% (at an annual rate)

findings.headline: The strategy caps each investment at £5m and total holding with any one institution at £10m.
findings.detail: These limits apply to the council's counterparty framework, which only permits sterling specified investments with UK government, other local authorities, or institutions rated highly by a credit rating agency. The counterparty list includes UK banks and building societies rated Fitch F1.
findings.matters: Counterparty limits define how much exposure a council accepts to a single bank, which is a point of comparison for peers and lenders.
findings.figures: £5m maximum investment amount; £10m maximum holding with any individual institution
findings.quote: Maximum holding with any individual institution £10m

findings.headline: Torridge expects slightly lower investment rates than the market because of its limited counterparty list and the size of its deposits.
findings.detail: The paper says the council's counterparty list is short and its deposit sizes are modest, so the rates available to it run slightly below market rates. It also notes some counterparties are not taking further deposits.
findings.matters: Smaller councils with narrow counterparty lists may face the same rate gap, which affects how much investment income they can expect.
findings.quote: Interest rates available to Torridge District Council will be slightly lower because of the limited names on Counterparty List and the size of the amounts that we invest.

findings.headline: Longer investment durations of 6 to 12 months were used in 2025/26, and the paper says this helped maintain investment income as rates fell.
findings.detail: The paper says the council placed investments for longer periods to maximise returns. It describes this as having helped maintain investment income while interest rates were falling.
findings.matters: Locking in longer deposits protects income in a falling-rate market, a strategy other councils with similar cash balances may weigh up against liquidity needs.
findings.figures: 6 to 12 months
findings.quote: With interest rates falling during the year this has helped maintain the investment income the council receives.

findings.headline: The Bank of England Bank Base Interest Rate was cut 3 times in 2025/26, from 4.50% to 3.75% by February 2026.
findings.detail: The paper describes the rate reductions during the year and says the market expects rates to ease slightly during 2026. Short-term rates are around 3.75% for three months.
findings.matters: Falling Bank Rate reduces investment income for every council holding cash, so the trend shapes budgets across the sector.
findings.quote: During 2025/26 the Bank of England Bank Base Interest Rate was cut 3 times from 4.50% at the start of the year, to 3.75% by February 2026.

findings.headline: The paper expects the level of investments to fall further in 2026/27 as capital expenditure continues.
findings.detail: Internal borrowing may be used to fund the capital programme, which would reduce the funds available for investment. The paper expects investment periods to be maintained while rates fall slightly.
findings.matters: A council drawing down investments to fund capital work faces a different liquidity and income profile from one holding cash balances.
findings.quote: It is anticipated that the level of investments will reduce further due to continued capital expenditure.

findings.headline: Short-term investments are estimated at approximately £28m at 31 March 2026, mostly made up of reserves and usable capital receipts.
findings.detail: The paper says the bulk of the investment balance represents reserves and usable capital receipts. The Capital Programme will be financed from capital receipts, grants, revenue contributions, reserves and borrowing, with internal borrowing possible.
findings.matters: Showing cash held in investments against reserves and capital receipts lets a reader judge how much of the council's liquidity is committed to planned capital spending.
findings.figures: approximately £28m
findings.quote: On 31st March 2026 short-term investments placed with financial institutions are estimated to be approximately £28m.

findings.headline: Long-term PWLB borrowing rates have increased during the year, with the 20-year loan rate now around 6.24%.
findings.detail: The paper says the 20-year PWLB rate has moved from just under 6.0% to around 6.24%. This raises the cost of any new borrowing in the programme.
findings.matters: A higher PWLB rate directly affects the cost of replacing funding and of new capital borrowing for councils with similar plans.
findings.figures: around 6.24%; just under 6.0%
findings.quote: Long-term borrowing rates from the PWLB have increased during the year.

findings.headline: The existing debt schedule was last reviewed for rescheduling or early redemption in 2017/18, when no advantage was found.
findings.detail: The paper states that the debt and loan schedule was considered in 2017/18 and concluded there was no advantage from re-scheduling or early redemption. It does not record a later review.
findings.matters: A finance director elsewhere can check whether a rate-based review of legacy debt has been repeated since rates moved, which this paper does not show.
findings.quote: The existing debt and loan schedule was considered in 2017/18 and it was concluded that there was no advantage from re-scheduling or early redemption of existing loans.

findings.headline: A borrowing figure of £1,095K for IFRS16 lease liabilities, mainly private sector housing leases, is included in the prudential indicators.
findings.detail: IFRS16 came into effect for local authorities on 1 April 2024 and brings material operating leases onto the balance sheet as lease liabilities. The paper says private sector housing leases make up most of the total.
findings.matters: Lease liabilities now sit within the borrowing measures, so they affect headline debt and prudential indicators for any council applying IFRS16.
findings.quote: A borrowing figure for these leases of £1,095K has been calculated and included in the prudential indicators.

findings.headline: The Prudential Indicators envisage substantial further long-term borrowing in 2026/27 for four named projects, with five approved borrowing schemes listed.
findings.detail: The paper lists approved borrowing for the Operational Services Centre, Town Hall Roof and Leisure Works, Appledore Maritime Innovation Centre, the Community Land Trust revolving loan fund and Hatchmoor Industrial Estate. Timing depends on project progress, the financial climate and internal resources.
findings.matters: A finance officer at another council can compare the scale of planned borrowing against its own capital programme and funding mix.
findings.figures: Operational Services Centre £2.8m; Town Hall Roof & Leisure Works £1.0m; Appledore Maritime Innovation Centre £1.1m; Community Land Trust (CLT) revolving loan fund £0.6m; Hatchmoor Industrial Estate £3.35m
findings.quote: The approved Prudential Indicators envisage that substantial further long-term borrowing may be undertaken in the year 2026/27 relating to the new Operational Service Centre, Town Hall Roof, Appledore Maritime Innovation Centre and Hatchmoor Industrial Estate.

findings.headline: Torridge's PWLB debt stands at £0.191m at 31 March 2026, with its last scheduled redemption due in March 2027.
findings.detail: The paper says no new long-term PWLB loans were taken out in 2025/26. The remaining £0.191m maturity loan is scheduled for settlement in March 2027.
findings.matters: The council's PWLB exposure is almost fully repaid, so any future borrowing will be new funding rather than refinancing of legacy PWLB debt.
findings.figures: £0.191m (PWLB borrowing at 31 March 2026); £0.191m (maturity loan settled March 2027)
findings.quote: Borrowings from PWLB at 31 March 2026 will total £0.191m. The next and last scheduled redemption occurs in March 2027 when a maturity type loan of £0.191m will be settled.

findings.headline: The risk section of the paper cites 96.5% as a reasonable collection estimate for 2026/27, while the body of the report gives 98.0% for that year.
findings.detail: The Risk Management section says a shortfall on the Collection Fund follows if the collection rate is not achieved. It then describes 96.5% as the reasonable estimate for 2026/27. The main text gives 98.0% for the same year, and the paper does not reconcile the two.
findings.matters: Two different collection assumptions for the same year bear directly on the size of any Collection Fund shortfall, which is the exposure a lender or finance director would want to size.
findings.figures: 96.5% (risk section, 2026/27); 98.0% (body of report, 2026/27); 97.0% (2027/28 estimate)
findings.quote: current performance indicates that 96.5% is a reasonable estimate for 2026/27.

findings.headline: Torridge estimates its 2027/28 council tax collection rate at 97.0%, against 98.0% in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The report says the Band D equivalents are reduced by a non-collection percentage based on current performance. The stated collection estimate for 2027/28 is lower than the 2026/27 figure the report gives. The tabled tax base will reflect the 97.0% rate.
findings.matters: A lower collection assumption reduces the council tax base and the income the council and its preceptors can budget for, and it is a direct change a finance director here or at a peer council would track.
findings.figures: 97.0% (2027/28 collection estimate); 98.0% (2026/27 collection estimate)
findings.quote: Based upon current performance the amount collected is estimated to be 97.0% (98.0% in 2026/27).

findings.headline: The paper describes ten schemes in the approved programme as undeliverable, but proposes removing nine
findings.detail: Paragraph 1.1 refers to ten schemes approved between 2012 and 2024 that cannot be delivered on their approved terms. Paragraph 2.1 proposes removing nine schemes, and the paper does not explain the difference.
findings.matters: A gap between the number of schemes described as undeliverable and the number removed is something a reader checking the council's capital approvals would want resolved.
findings.figures: 10 schemes described in 1.1; 9 schemes proposed for removal in 2.1
findings.quote: It includes ten schemes, approved between 2012 and 2024, that can no longer be delivered on the terms on which they were approved.

findings.headline: The paper says the programme retains £6.2m of housing capital, or £8.7m including a £2,533k Disabled Facilities Grant
findings.detail: The retained housing items include Local Authority Housing Fund Round 4 (£2,156k), Private Sector Leases (£1,500k) and Support Programme for Social Housing stock to improve EPC (£1,500k). Homelessness Accommodation at Hubbastone and modulars is £357k.
findings.matters: The split between retained housing commitments and the removed schemes shows where a council's remaining capital is concentrated.
findings.figures: £6.2m housing capital excluding DFG; £8.7m including DFG; £2,533k DFG; £2,156k LAHF Round 4; £1,500k Private Sector Leases
findings.quote: The programme retains £6.2m of housing capital, excluding the Disabled Facilities Grant

findings.headline: The paper states that cost estimates set in 2012 or 2017 cannot deliver the same works today
findings.detail: The paper says any of the removed schemes brought forward now would need to return to Council for approval at a revised sum. It presents removal as the route to reducing borrowing rather than carrying the schemes forward.
findings.matters: Approvals made years earlier at historic costs can understate what the same works cost now, which affects other councils' capital approvals made on similar terms.
findings.figures: 2012 and 2017 cost estimates
findings.quote: Cost estimates set in 2012 or 2017 cannot deliver the same works today.

findings.headline: Three approved schemes totalling £250k were never delivered, the oldest approved in 2012
findings.detail: Group B comprises Decent Homes Funding (2012, £127k), Barton House Hostel Re-modelling (2017, £77k) and Sandymere Road (2022, £46k). The paper says removal does not remove the underlying need, and that any scheme revived would need a current costing and design.
findings.matters: Approvals that sit undelivered for more than a decade show how a council's capital programme can carry budget with no spending plan behind it.
findings.figures: £250k Group B total; £127k Decent Homes Funding; £77k Barton House; £46k Sandymere Road
findings.quote: Group B: three schemes, £250k, that were never delivered. The oldest was approved in 2012.

findings.headline: Capital funding available is £52,207k against a £50,580k approved programme, a programme surplus of £1,627k
findings.detail: After £831k of timing on the vehicle replacement programme is excluded, a general surplus of £796k remains. Of that, £489k is applied to reduce borrowing and £307k is retained for urgent capital needs and inflation.
findings.matters: A surplus that can be applied to reduce borrowing, rather than to fund new schemes, is a specific capital position a finance director can compare with their own programme.
findings.figures: £52,207k funding available; £50,580k approved programme; £1,627k programme surplus; £831k vehicle timing; £796k general surplus; £489k applied to borrowing; £307k retained
findings.quote: Funding available for the programme exceeds the approved programme, giving a surplus.

findings.headline: The paper proposes reducing the council's borrowing requirement by £0.9m, estimated to save £100k a year
findings.detail: The £0.9m is funded from the £411k released by the removals and £489k of the general programme surplus. The paper estimates the annual saving as £60k of interest at 6% and £40k of MRP over 25 years.
findings.matters: Lower borrowing reduces both interest and MRP, which is the revenue effect a finance officer at another council or a lender would look for in a capital clean-up.
findings.figures: £0.9m borrowing reduction; £100k a year saving; £60k interest at 6%; £40k MRP over 25 years; £489k applied from surplus; £411k from removals
findings.quote: Reducing borrowing by £1m saves an estimated £100k a year

findings.headline: Torridge proposes removing nine capital schemes totalling £411k from a £50,580k approved programme, six of them complete or acquired and three never delivered
findings.detail: The paper proposes removing nine schemes: six where works are complete or assets acquired (£161k) and three never delivered (£250k). It states that removal requires Full Council approval.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender sees a council clearing dormant capital approvals from its programme, which changes the programme's size and the borrowing it implies.
findings.figures: £50,580k approved programme; £411k removed; £161k Group A; £250k Group B
findings.quote: Remove the nine schemes, totalling £411k, from the capital programme

findings.headline: Total Council Tax Reduction cost for 2026/27 is stated as over £4.8 million, split across pension-age and working-age caseloads of 1,886 and 1,964 customers.
findings.detail: The report gives the 2026/27 cost of the scheme for both pension-age and working-age customers. It shows the pension-age caseload at £2,791,851.51 and the working-age caseload at £2,092,205.16. The cost is shared between preceptors.
findings.matters: The scale of the scheme relative to the billing authority's own share is a benchmark other councils can compare with their own reduction-scheme costs.
findings.quote: The total cost of Council Tax Reduction for both pension age customers and working age customers during 2026/27 is over £4.8 million

findings.headline: Raising the working-age income bands by 6.7% for 2027/28 is modelled to add circa £119,547.18 to the scheme cost, of which circa £13,150.19 falls on Torridge at 11%.
findings.detail: The report says the 6.7% uplift is intended to align with the Autumn Statement increases of 3.9% to the National Minimum Wage and 3.5% to most working-age benefits. Costs are shared mainly with the preceptors, Devon County Council, Police and Fire, so Torridge's share is small. The modelling uses current circumstances and excludes individual income increases.
findings.matters: A finance officer elsewhere would see how a council sizes the cost of an income-band uplift and how that cost is apportioned between billing authority and precepting bodies.
findings.quote: the actual costs for Torridge based on the 11%, including Parish Councils, is circa £13,150.19.

findings.headline: Torridge's Council Tax Reduction Scheme no longer has a specific government grant, having been folded into the general Government grant.
findings.detail: The report states the council no longer receives a dedicated grant for the scheme. Funding for it now sits within the general Government grant. The report gives no figure for the amount now treated as covering the scheme.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or elsewhere, would want to know that a scheme cost is no longer separately identifiable in grant income and now competes within general funding.
findings.quote: The Council no longer receives a specific grant for the Council Tax Reduction Scheme as it is now included within the general Government grant.

findings.paper_title: 12 - Mid Year Review of Treasury Management
findings.headline: The Bank of England base rate increased to 4.0% in November 2026.
findings.detail: The paper describes this as the first rise after the cuts to 3.75%. It says further inflation-driven rises may be expected in the short term, and forecasts the base rate at 4.25% by the end of 2026/27.
findings.matters: A rise in base rate would lift the return on short-term deposits, which the council's forecasts do not yet reflect.
findings.figures: 4.0% base rate from November 2026; 4.25% forecast year-end 2026/27
findings.quote: In November 2026 the BOE base rate increased to 4.0%.

findings.paper_title: 12 - Mid Year Review of Treasury Management
findings.headline: The council's remaining PWLB debt of £191k is due to be paid off on 31 March 2027.
findings.detail: The paper lists this as the council's only outstanding Public Works Loan Board debt. It does not say whether the loan will be repaid early or at maturity.
findings.matters: A council with no remaining PWLB debt after March 2027 has no further scheduled loan repayments or refinancing to manage.
findings.figures: £191k outstanding; repayment date 31st March 2027
findings.quote: The Council currently has Public Works Loan Board debt of £191k outstanding which will be paid off on 31st March 2027.

findings.paper_title: 12 - Mid Year Review of Treasury Management
findings.headline: Forecast 2026/27 bank account interest is £500k, against £407k received in 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper reports bank interest separately from interest on short-term investments. The forecast rise is in the opposite direction to the forecast fall in investment return.
findings.matters: A finance director comparing treasury income across councils would want to see bank interest and deposit interest reported separately, as Torridge does here.
findings.quote: this is forecasted for 2026/27 to be £500k, which compares to £407k received in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: 12 - Mid Year Review of Treasury Management
findings.headline: Short-term investments lodged with financial institutions are £23m, against £33m at the same point last year.
findings.detail: The paper gives the current balance of short-term investments and the comparable figure for the same time in the previous year. It does not give a reason for the change.
findings.matters: A fall in cash held on short-term deposit reduces the council's available liquidity and the income it earns from that cash.
findings.figures: £23m current; £33m same time last year
findings.quote: Currently the Council has short term investments of £23m lodged with financial institutions, the comparable figure for the same time last year being £33m.

findings.paper_title: 12 - Mid Year Review of Treasury Management
findings.headline: Average return on short-term investments is 4.30% for 2026/27, down from 4.52% in 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper links the reduction to the base rate cuts that brought the base rate to 3.75%. It presents the change as a movement in the average rate earned on the council's short-term investments.
findings.matters: The gap between the average rate and the base rate shows the council's yield on its cash, which other finance officers can compare against their own.
findings.quote: slightly reduced the average rate of return earned by the Council on its short term investments to 4.30% from 4.52% in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: 12 - Mid Year Review of Treasury Management
findings.headline: Forecast 2026/27 return from short-term investments is £700k, against £1,430k in 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the fall to the Bank of England base rate cuts between August 2024 and December 2025, which took the base rate to 3.75%. The Lead Member's comment states that the strategy is delivering a reasonable rate of return.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council would want to compare how far a fall in base rate has reduced investment income for a council of this size.
findings.quote: The forecast return from short term investments for 2026/27 is £700k, which compares with a return of £1,430k in 2025/26.

findings.headline: The Northam Burrows additional income is included in a £300k estimate covering car parking and Burrows charges
findings.detail: The paper says the additional income from the Burrows change is not stated separately but is counted within a combined £300k estimate for car parking and Burrows charges. The paper does not give a separate figure for the Burrows element.
findings.matters: A finance director would want to know that the saving is bundled into a single estimate, so the Burrows contribution cannot be tracked separately against the budget gap.
findings.figures: £300k estimate for car parking and Burrows charges
findings.quote: The additional income is included in the £300k estimate for car parking and Burrows charges.

findings.headline: Torridge proposes a summer charge of £10 at Northam Burrows for June, July and August from 1 April 2027, up from £8
findings.detail: The paper proposes a £10 summer charge for June to August, aligned with the new car parking summer season. The spring/autumn charge stays at £8 and the November to March period stays free. The paper notes an earlier option of £9 standard and £11 summer was considered, and that this proposal keeps the standard charge unchanged.
findings.matters: It is one of the income measures put forward to close a 2027/28 budget gap, and a finance director elsewhere may compare how seasonal, peak-targeted charging is being used as a budget lever.
findings.figures: £8 (2026/27 summer and spring/autumn), £10 (2027/28 summer), +£2 change; standard charge £8 unchanged
findings.quote: From 1 April 2027, introduce a summer charge of £10 for June, July and August, aligned with the new car parking summer season.

findings.headline: The paper is framed as a proposal to reduce the 2027/28 budget gap, with a post-implementation review of demand and income due in Q3 2027/28.
findings.detail: The paper is a Member Budget Working Group proposal to Full Council on 7 December 2026. It commits to a post-implementation review of demand and income in the third quarter of 2027/28, which is the point at which the projected yield can be tested.
findings.matters: A scheduled check on whether a budget-gap measure delivers its estimated income is the kind of commitment a lender or finance director would follow up.
findings.quote: A post-implementation review of demand and income will be carried out in the third quarter of 2027/28.

findings.headline: Torridge car parking income is over £2m a year, a record high, from more than 770,000 visits a year.
findings.detail: The paper reports that car parking income is over £2m a year and at a record high, and that visits have grown by 20,000 in two years. It also notes that the 2026/27 Westward Ho! hourly rate rose 11% to £2.00 with no visible fall in demand.
findings.matters: Evidence that demand held after a price rise is the basis for the proposed increases, and a finance officer elsewhere could compare it with their own discretionary parking yields.
findings.figures: over £2m a year; more than 770,000 visits a year; up 20,000 in two years; Westward Ho! rate rose by 11% to £2.00
findings.quote: Income is over £2m a year, a record high, from more than 770,000 visits a year, up 20,000 in two years.

findings.headline: Torridge estimates the combined Northam Burrows and car parking changes will raise £300k a year from 2027/28.
findings.detail: Paragraph 2.4 states that together with the Northam Burrows proposal in Appendix 2, the changes are estimated to raise £300k a year. The paper does not separate the car parking element from the Northam Burrows element.
findings.matters: It quantifies the savings the council is relying on to close its 2027/28 budget gap, which a lender or peer council would want to test against actual outturn.
findings.figures: £300k a year from 2027/28
findings.quote: the changes are estimated to raise £300k a year from 2027/28.

findings.headline: Torridge proposes three-season car parking charges at Westward Ho! and Appledore from 1 April 2027, with summer hourly rates rising to £2.60 and £2.20.
findings.detail: The paper sets out a split of the year into summer (June to August), spring/autumn (April, May, September, October) and winter (November to March), replacing the current seven-month summer tariff. Table 1 shows Westward Ho! summer rising from £2.00 to £2.60 and Appledore summer from £1.60 to £2.20.
findings.matters: Car parking is described as the council's largest discretionary income stream, so a tariff redesign to raise income from visitors is a concrete budget lever a finance director or lender would track.
findings.figures: Westward Ho! summer £2.00 to £2.60 (+60p); Westward Ho! spring/autumn £2.00 to £2.40 (+40p); Appledore summer £1.60 to £2.20 (+60p); Appledore spring/autumn £1.60 to £1.80 (+20p); Together with Northam Burrows, estimated £300k a year from 2027/28
findings.quote: Introduce three seasons from 1 April 2027 (Figure 1)

findings.headline: The paper says the £86k income estimate depends on subscriber numbers holding up after the increase.
findings.detail: The paper states that the income estimate depends on subscriber numbers after the increase. Subscribers will be told of the new charge before 2027/28 renewals. The paper does not give current subscriber numbers or a sensitivity figure.
findings.matters: The yield from a subscription service is exposed to customer loss when prices rise, so the assumption is one a finance director would test against actual renewal numbers.
findings.figures: £86k a year estimated additional income
findings.quote: The income estimate depends on subscriber numbers holding up after the increase.

findings.headline: Torridge proposes raising its annual garden waste subscription from £57 to £67 for 2027/28, estimated to raise an additional £86k a year.
findings.detail: The working group compared the charge with neighbouring councils and proposes aligning it with North Devon Council's expected £67 for 2027/28. The paper says the increase equates to around £1.29 a week and is estimated to raise £86k a year. The proposal is a recommendation to Full Council on 7 December 2026.
findings.matters: A discretionary fee increase is one of the specific measures offered to close a 2027/28 budget gap, and finance officers at other councils will want to compare the size of the yield and the pricing benchmark used.
findings.figures: £57 (2026/27 subscription); £67 (proposed 2027/28 subscription); £10 increase; £86k a year additional income; £1.29 a week
findings.quote: Increase the annual garden waste subscription from £57 to £67 for 2027/28, an increase of £10.

findings.headline: Short-term borrowing maturity at 55% exceeds prudential target of 30%, though council explains this reflects its small scale
findings.detail: The maturity structure shows 55% of fixed-rate borrowing due within 12 months, 25 percentage points above the 30% upper target. The council's outstanding PWLB borrowing is only £191k, with other borrowing reflecting IFRS 16 lease liabilities. The council notes this deviation is structural—small authorities with few loans find it difficult to meet the maturity targets designed for larger authorities.
findings.matters: Maturity structure is a key prudential indicator. Concentration of repayments in the short term creates refinancing risk, though the council's explanation suggests this is a composition issue rather than a borrowing risk problem.
findings.figures: Under 12 months 55% actual vs 30% upper target; £191k PWLB borrowing outstanding
findings.quote: Torridge currently only has £191k outstanding in loans due to PWLB in 2025/26. Other borrowing relates to the recognitions of future Right of Use lease liabilities recognised under IFRS 16.

findings.headline: Financing costs achieved net interest income benefit of £21.93 per Band D property against estimated cost of £39.43
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream was -14.69% actual (2025-26), meaning interest income exceeded borrowing costs. This contrasts sharply with -1.11% estimate. The council's treasury operations delivered a net saving of £21.93 per Band D property across 26,408 properties, a £61 per property swing from the budgeted cost position.
findings.matters: The scale of variance (£39.43 cost estimated becoming £21.93 saving actual) indicates either significant treasury outperformance or material changes in interest rate environment that affected the council's net interest position. Both matter to finance directors and those assessing financial management quality.
findings.figures: Financing costs -£1,744,000; ratio -14.69% actual vs -1.11% estimate; per Band D property -£21.93 actual vs £39.43 estimate; 26,408 Band D equivalent properties
findings.quote: The impact of the decrease in net financing costs when spread across the 26,408 band D equivalent properties in the Borough equates to £21.93 per property per annum.

findings.headline: No additional external borrowing undertaken in 2025-26 despite capital spending rising to £19.6m and CFR reaching £3.9m
findings.detail: The council managed capital spending of £19.6m and a capital financing requirement of £3.9m without new external borrowing, instead using existing debt capacity, grants (£11.3m), revenue contributions (£5.7m), and internal resources (£2.2m internal borrowing). This contrasts with the estimate which assumed £5.4m of internal borrowing.
findings.matters: Borrowing decisions matter to lenders. A council choosing not to seek new external financing when CFR is materially present signals confidence in existing cash position and reduced future refinancing requirements.
findings.figures: No new external borrowing; total capital spending £19,589k; CFR £3,901k; internal borrowing used £2,152k against estimate of £5,417k
findings.quote: No additional external borrowing was undertaken during 2025/26. Actual borrowing for the year as shown above, is significantly below the Authorised limit.

findings.headline: Capital programme underspent by 50% at £19.6m against £39m budget, with delays to Town Hall project
findings.detail: Actual capital expenditure was £19.6m compared to estimate of £38.9m. The council attributes this to delays in capital projects, particularly the Town Hall. This represents material slippage in capital programme delivery affecting both timing and scope of planned works.
findings.matters: Lenders assess capital programme delivery as an indicator of execution capability and financial control. A 50% variance signals project delivery risk or scope changes that affect council finances and debt servicing.
findings.figures: Actual £19,589k; Estimate £38,978k; variance £19,389k (50%)
findings.quote: The variance between actual and estimated capital expenditure is due to the delay in spend on capital projects such as the Town Hall.

findings.headline: Base rate static at 3.75% since December 2025; further reductions may pressure investment income given Bank of England's 2% inflation target
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that further reductions in the base rate may pressure investment returns. Rates have been static at 3.75% since December 2025, but with the BoE targeting 2% inflation, the trajectory points downward. The £1.4m investment income achieved this year assumes current or higher rates and may not be sustainable.
findings.matters: A finance director must budget for scenario where this year's £1.85m total interest income declines; a lender needs to understand whether the council's financial plan remains stable if investment yield falls materially.
findings.figures: Base rate 3.75% (static since December 2025); BoE inflation target 2%
findings.quote: Further reductions in the bank rate may place pressure on investment returns in future given the Bank of England's 2% inflation target.

findings.headline: Lease obligations of £402k added to balance sheet for temporary accommodation and car park
findings.detail: Under IFRS 16 accounting, the council has £402k in recognized lease obligations. These are specifically for private sector leases providing temporary accommodation and the Quay Car Park. While small, these represent genuine future cash commitments separate from traditional PWLB debt that lenders must factor into total debt burden assessment.
findings.matters: IFRS 16 leases create real future liabilities; a finance director and lender need total debt visibility, including leases, not just PWLB. The temporary accommodation element flags demand-driven cost pressure.
findings.figures: £402k lease obligation balance
findings.quote: In addition to the outstanding loans to PWLB, under accounting standard IFRS16 Torridge has a balance outstanding of £402k relating to lease obligations for Right of Use Assets, significantly these are Private Sector Leases for properties to provide temporary accommodation and the Quay Car Park.

findings.headline: PWLB debt position minimal at £191k with no repayments made in year
findings.detail: Torridge carries only £191k of Public Works Loan Board debt. The council made no debt repayments during 2025/26, indicating it is managing down a very small residual balance or has no active borrowing needs. This is an exceptionally strong debt position.
findings.matters: Debt service capacity is the foundation of lender risk assessment; a council with only £191k PWLB debt has minimal refinancing or default risk.
findings.figures: £191k outstanding at 31 March 2026; no repayments made in 2025/26
findings.quote: During 2025/26 there were no repayments made on long term Public Loans Board debt, the balance outstanding at the close of 2025/26 was £191k.

findings.headline: Liquid reserves grew 40% to £28m in a single year
findings.detail: The council substantially increased its short-term investments from £20m to £28m. Combined with minimal PWLB debt (£191k), this demonstrates very strong liquidity and financial flexibility, suggesting either improved cash generation or a deliberate build of reserves.
findings.matters: Lenders assess liquidity as a measure of financial stability and resilience; growth in investment balances reduces future borrowing dependency.
findings.figures: £28m (31 March 2026) vs £20m (31 March 2025); increase of £8m
findings.quote: As at the 31st March 2026 the Council had short term investments of £28m lodged with financial institutions, the comparable figure for the 31st March 2025 being £20m.

findings.headline: Investment returns grew 72% to £1,430k despite interest rates falling from 5.35% to 4.52%
findings.detail: Short-term investment returns increased significantly from £831k to £1,430k by deploying substantially more cash into investments. The council's total investment balance grew from £20m to £28m. Although the yield on each pound invested declined with falling interest rates, the larger capital base generated material additional income.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the sustainability of the council's investment income, which underpins its financial position; further rate cuts would erode this gain.
findings.figures: £1,430k (2025/26) vs £831k (2024/25), average rate 4.52% vs 5.35%, investments £28m vs £20m
findings.quote: The return from short term investments in 2025/26 was £1,430k, which is an increase of £599k from £831k in 2024/25.

findings.headline: Rough sleeper services funding faces cessation risk from 2026/27 with no continuation plan stated
findings.detail: The council is delivering rough sleeper services valued at approximately £70,031 (RSI Initiative), £25,125 (Winter Pressures Move On Worker), and £45,472 (RSAP accommodation support) totalling £140,628 in 2025/26 through Encompass Southwest under procurement waivers. All three funding streams are temporary government grants from MHCLG. The council explicitly states it will review service provision only once clarity emerges from MHCLG on funding arrangements from 2026/27 onwards, indicating no contingency planning is currently underway.
findings.matters: A material service (£140k+) dependent entirely on time-limited government grants faces discontinuation unless funding is renewed; the council has not articulated either a continuation strategy or fallback funding source, creating financial and service delivery uncertainty from 2027 onwards.
findings.figures: £70,031 RSI services, £25,125 Winter Pressures funding, £45,472 RSAP revenue = £140,628 in 2025/26; RSI funded as extension to original 3-year allocation; all other streams ad hoc or temporary
findings.quote: Once there is some clarity from MHCLG over funding arrangements from 2026/27, we will review our services to rough sleepers.

findings.headline: Strong cash position now (£35.3m) but projected to decline to £18m within one year.
findings.detail: As at 31 March 2026, the council held £23.4m in short-term investments plus £11.9m in the current bank account. The council projects this will fall to circa £18m by 31 March 2027. While expressing confidence in meeting obligations, this trajectory reflects ongoing reserve drawdown to fund operational deficits.
findings.matters: The declining cash position, combined with the structural deficit, shows the council is already in drawdown mode. At current deficit rates, reserves would be significantly depleted by the early 2030s, tightening liquidity and financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £35.3m total cash as at 31 March 2026 (£23.4m short-term investments, £11.9m current account); projected £18m by 31 March 2027
findings.quote: The Council is predicting to have cash balances of circa £18m (current bank account and short-term treasury deposits) as at the 31st March 2027 and is therefore confident it can meet its financial obligations for the foreseeable future.

findings.headline: All PWLB borrowing repaid; zero long-term debt outstanding as at end of 2025/26.
findings.detail: Torridge has repaid its final Public Works Loan Board loan, leaving zero long-term borrowing commitments. The report presents this as a positive, noting only a very small proportion of revenue budget goes to capital financing costs.
findings.matters: While debt-free appears positive, for a council facing a growing £7.265m revenue deficit, the absence of an established PWLB relationship or credit line could limit borrowing options if deficits accelerate. It also signals the council has not drawn on long-term capital finance in recent years.
findings.figures: Zero long-term borrowing as at close of 2025/26; prior debts held with Public Works Loan Board
findings.quote: The balance of long-term borrowing commitments all held with the Public Works Loan Board at the close of the financial year 2026/27 was zero, the final loan having been repaid in the year.

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation demand flagged as uncontrolled and ongoing cost risk.
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation is explicitly identified as a financial risk that could increase further, alongside capital programme cost overruns and pay inflation. The paper provides no quantification of current spend or trajectory, indicating it is an emerging area of concern.
findings.matters: Temporary Accommodation is typically the fastest-growing and least controllable cost line for councils. Uncontrolled TA demand can rapidly deplete reserves and trigger unexpected budget pressures beyond forecasts.
findings.figures: No figures provided in this report
findings.quote: In particular the costs of delivering the capital programme could increase beyond the funding envelope, demand for Temporary Accommodation could increase further and pay and non-pay inflation could again return.

findings.headline: A £7.265m cumulative funding gap over 2026/27–2030/31 with only £2.001m in Budgetary Stabilisation Reserve to cover it.
findings.detail: The council's Medium Term Financial Strategy shows growing annual revenue deficits: £0.399m in 2026/27 rising to £1.932m by 2030/31. The Budgetary Stabilisation Reserve can cover only the first two years of deficits (£1.760m), leaving a £5.505m gap from 2028/29 onwards that must be closed through identified savings or new income. The paper states the council will "continue to seek operational efficiencies and new income streams in order to bring the Council's finances back into balance and therefore avoid the need to drain the Budgetary Stabilisation Reserve."
findings.matters: A structural revenue deficit that cannot be funded by existing reserves without new decisions represents material solvency risk. Without identified solutions, the council exhausts its financial buffer and faces potential financial distress.
findings.figures: £7.265m cumulative deficit; annual deficits of £0.399m (2026/27), £1.361m (2027/28), £1.679m (2028/29), £1.894m (2029/30), £1.932m (2030/31); Budgetary Stabilisation Reserve £2.001m as at 1st April 2026
findings.quote: There is therefore only enough resources in the Budgetary Stabilisation reserve to meet the cumulative deficit anticipated for the next two financial years.
